# Solana Developer Platform

> Full public documentation for Solana Developer Platform — all page content for AI and agent ingestion.

## Canonical URLs
- Docs: https://platform.solana.com/docs
- API: https://api.solana.com
- Interactive API docs: https://api.solana.com/docs
- OpenAPI: https://api.solana.com/openapi.json
- AI guide: https://platform.solana.com/docs/reference/docs-for-ai

## Docs

### What is SDP?
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/introduction

> One API for tokenization, custody, payments, and compliance on Solana.

SDP provides tokenization, custody, payments, and compliance through one stable API in front of interchangeable providers. Operations use project-scoped authentication.

| Module | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Issuance** | Deploy, mint, burn, freeze, pause, and seize tokens built on Token-2022 |
| **Custody** | Provision and operate Solana wallets through interchangeable custody providers |
| **Payments** | Move funds onchain — transfers, batches, recurring payments, payment requests, and ramps |
| **Compliance** | Screen wallets and transactions against your regulatory program |

## Background

Institutional capital is moving onchain: [$35 billion in tokenized real-world assets](https://app.rwa.xyz/) across public blockchains, [$3.2 billion of it on Solana](https://app.rwa.xyz/networks/solana), and [tokenized stocks](https://app.rwa.xyz/stocks) — where Solana settles most trading volume — as the fastest-growing slice.

Assets at this scale need regulated custody, enforceable compliance, and auditable controls. SDP provides them as one API, so bringing an asset onchain does not require a team of Solana developers.

## Core Features

<Steps>
<Step>
### Unified Programming Interface

SDP puts one stable API in front of the Solana ecosystem's providers, so you integrate once and swap or add providers without changing your code. The same onramp call works for every ramp provider. The `provider` field is the only thing that changes.

<Tabs items={["JavaScript", "Python", "curl"]}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```javascript title="onramp-quote.js" rotate-providers
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/quote",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      provider: "moonpay",
      counterpartyId: "cp_...",
      destinationCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_...",
      assetRail: "usdc.solana",
      fiatCurrency: "USD",
      fiatAmount: "100.00",
    }),
  },
);
const quote = await response.json();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Python">
```python title="onramp_quote.py" rotate-providers

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/quote",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_..."},
    json={
        "provider": "moonpay",
        "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
        "destinationCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_...",
        "assetRail": "usdc.solana",
        "fiatCurrency": "USD",
        "fiatAmount": "100.00",
    },
)
quote = response.json()
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal" rotate-providers
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/ramps/onramp/quote \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "provider": "moonpay",
    "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
    "destinationCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_...",
    "assetRail": "usdc.solana",
    "fiatCurrency": "USD",
    "fiatAmount": "100.00"
  }'
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>
</Step>
<Step>
### Wallet Custody

Provision signing wallets through integrated custody providers, so your team never handles private keys. Hosted keys never leave the provider's MPC or TEE infrastructure and SDP only handles the signed transaction. Local development keys are encrypted at rest with `AES-256-GCM` using per-organization derived keys, and every signing request passes authentication, permission and allowed-operation checks before it executes.

- **Built on `@solana/keychain`**

   The unified Solana signing interface. Every custody backend is a keychain adapter behind the same signing API, which is what makes providers interchangeable.

- **[Allowed operations](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#allowed-operations)**

   Limit what an API key may do. List the operation families and types a key may perform, and every other operation is refused before it executes.

- **Scoped custody configuration**

   Custody settings resolve per project, then organization, then environment, so different teams can run different providers side by side.
</Step>
<Step>
### Issuance and Compliance with Token-2022

Create tokens from pre-built templates (stablecoin, tokenized security) or configure your own using Token-2022 extensions. Deploy, mint, burn, and manage supply through the dashboard or API.

Those same extensions are what make compliance enforceable onchain. Freeze individual accounts, pause token activity, seize tokens, and manage each token's **Token Access Control** list for regulated issuance flows. Selected compliance actions accept reason or memo fields for audit trails. Every enforcement action is one POST on the same token surface.

<Tabs items={["JavaScript", "Python", "curl"]}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```javascript title="compliance-action.js" rotate-token-ops
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/freeze",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(operationParams),
  },
);
const result = await response.json();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Python">
```python title="compliance_action.py" rotate-token-ops

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/freeze",
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_..."},
    json=operation_params,
)
result = response.json()
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal" rotate-token-ops
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_abc123/freeze \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "$OPERATION_PARAMS"
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>
</Step>
<Step>
### Ramps and Onchain Transfers

SDP exposes unified endpoints for onchain transfers and ramps across providers, built on official Solana program implementations like [Subscriptions](https://github.com/solana-program/subscriptions) and [Solana Pay](https://github.com/solana-foundation/pay). These power Recurring Payments, Payment Requests, and Batch Transfers within SDP.

<Tabs items={["Recurring Payments", "Payment Requests", "Batch Transfers"]}>
<Tab value="Recurring Payments">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/recurring-payments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_123",
    "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
    "counterpartyAccountId": "cpa_...",
    "token": "USDC",
    "amount": "25.00",
    "periodHours": 720
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Payment Requests">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/requests \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "walletId": "privy_wallet_123",
    "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
    "token": "USDC",
    "amount": "25.00",
    "expiresAt": "2026-08-31T00:00:00.000Z"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Batch Transfers">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfer-batches \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "externalId": "payroll_2026_06_30",
    "sourceCustodyWalletId": "cwlt_example",
    "token": "USDC",
    "recipients": [
      {
        "externalId": "payroll_row_001",
        "counterpartyId": "cp_...",
        "counterpartyAccountId": "cpa_...",
        "amount": "25.00"
      }
    ]
  }'
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The same API extends to on/offramps: rate estimates, quotes, and settlement work identically across every provider and corridor, so money can enter as fiat, live onchain as a token you issued, and exit back to fiat: a complete lifecycle from issuance through circulation to redemption, without stitching together provider-specific integrations. See [Payments](/docs/payments) for transfers and [Ramps](/docs/payments/ramps) for supported providers, currencies, and corridors.
</Step>
<Step>
### Audit Trails

Every sensitive operation is recorded automatically. Each entry captures the acting user or API key, the resource touched, success or failure, client IP, user agent, request id, and secret-redacted metadata, and is queryable per organization.

| Area                    | Recorded events                                                                    |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| API keys                | Create, revoke, and rotate, for both organization and project-scoped keys          |
| Token issuance          | Deploy, mint, burn, force-burn, supply changes, and authority updates              |
| Compliance actions      | Freeze, unfreeze, pause, unpause, seize, and Token Access Control changes          |
| Custody                 | Provider configuration, wallet provisioning, and credential lifecycle changes      |
| Transactions & signing  | Signing requests, submissions, and failed submissions                              |
| Organization & access   | Members, invitations, projects, and project membership             |
| Counterparties & assets | Counterparty and Counterparty Account changes, asset profile changes               |
</Step>
</Steps>

---

## Developing with SDP

### Overview
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp

> The interfaces, environments, and conventions you build against.

SDP exposes two interfaces that operate over the same backend and enforce the same permissions and audit trails:

- **Dashboard** — browser-based UI for setup, token management, and compliance operations. Sign in with email, Google, or GitHub.
- **REST API:** programmatic access for backend integrations. Routes authenticate with an API key in the `Authorization` header.

Everything the dashboard does is available through the API. Build against the API for automation and integrations; use the dashboard to set up your organization, inspect state, and perform one-off operations. An API key's [allowed operations](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#allowed-operations) restrict only requests made with that key, not dashboard sessions.

## Environments

The environment is a property of the **project**, not of individual requests. Every organization has exactly two projects, one sandbox and one production. Every tenant resource and API key belongs to one of them and inherits that project's environment.

| Project      | Network      | API key prefix |
| ------------ | ------------ | -------------- |
| `sandbox`    | devnet       | `sk_test_`     |
| `production` | mainnet-beta | `sk_live_`     |

Both environments use the same base URL, `https://api.solana.com`, and the same route shapes. The API key you send decides the project, and with it the environment. Develop and test against the sandbox project, then move to production with a production key.

Resources don't carry over between projects: the production project has its own wallets, tokens, and API keys, so set those up there before you go live. Production access is enabled per organization; see [Set Up Your Organization & Projects](/docs/guides/setup-organization).

## Response conventions

Every successful response wraps its payload in a `data` envelope with request metadata:

```json
{
  "data": { ... },
  "meta": { "requestId": "req_...", "timestamp": "2026-07-31T12:00:00.000Z" }
}
```

Errors return a machine-readable `code` alongside a human-readable `message`:

```json
{
  "error": { "code": "INVALID_API_KEY", "message": "Invalid API key" }
}
```

Include the `requestId` when reporting an issue — it links your request to our internal traces and audit records.

## Execution model

Most operations are server-executed: SDP builds the transaction, signs it with a custody wallet in your project, submits it, and records the result. A smaller set of issuance routes, marked by `prepare` in the path, return an unsigned transaction instead, which you sign and submit yourself. See [Signing modes](/docs/developing-with-sdp/signing-modes) for which operations support each mode and how they differ.

---

### Idempotency
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency

> Replay-safe mutations through the Idempotency-Key header, claimed by the record itself.

Retries are a fact of distributed systems: clients time out, connections drop, workers die mid-run. SDP lets you replay a mutation safely by sending an `Idempotency-Key` header — a unique value (a UUID works well) that you mint once per logical operation and reuse on every retry of that operation.

```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/payments/transfers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 8a2f6c1e-9d4b-4f3a-b7e5-2c8d9f0a1b3c" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ ... }'
```

## How replay resolution works

SDP's model differs from response-cache designs: the idempotency key is claimed by the **business record itself**, not by a snapshot of the original response.

1. The first request creates the record — a transfer, a batch, an issuance transaction — carrying your key and a fingerprint of the normalized request payload.
2. A retry with the same key and the same payload returns **HTTP 200 with the stored record**, in the normal success envelope. Because it is the live record and not a cached response, a replay reflects current state — a transfer that has since finalized comes back `finalized`, not the `processing` you would have seen on the first attempt. Freeze and unfreeze differ in one case: replaying one whose original attempt failed returns **400** with the original error.
3. A request with the same key but a **different payload** is rejected with **409 `CONFLICT`** ("Idempotency key already used with different request payload"). For transfers and batches, a different source wallet also counts as a different payload. The fingerprint comparison is field-normalized, so formatting differences don't cause false conflicts.

A replay still goes through the route's permission and [allowed operations](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#allowed-operations) checks first. If the key no longer has them, the retry gets the `403`, not the stored record.

Keys are retained for the lifetime of the record they claimed — there is no TTL, and a replay works for as long as the record exists. If a mint fails before anything is submitted on-chain, though, SDP releases the key, so a retry with the same key runs as a new request.

The header is optional. Every `/v1` route validates it when present (1–255 printable ASCII characters, otherwise `400 BAD_REQUEST`) and echoes it back on the response, but among the public endpoints only the operations below consume it. Elsewhere it is accepted and ignored.

## Where it applies

These twelve operations accept an `Idempotency-Key`. Each domain claims keys in its own namespace, and the namespaces are scoped differently:

| Operation | Endpoint | Key namespace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create a transfer | `POST /v1/payments/transfers` | Per project |
| Create a transfer batch | `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches` | Per project |
| Deploy a token | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/deploy` | Issuance, per organization |
| Mint | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/mint` | Issuance, per organization |
| Burn | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/burn` | Issuance, per organization |
| Force-burn | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/force-burn` | Issuance, per organization |
| Seize | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/seize` | Issuance, per organization |
| Freeze an account | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/freeze` | Issuance, per organization |
| Unfreeze an account | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/unfreeze` | Issuance, per organization |
| Pause token transfers | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/pause` | Issuance, per organization |
| Unpause token transfers | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/unpause` | Issuance, per organization |
| Update an authority | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/authority` | Issuance, per organization |

Namespaces are independent across domains — the same key value used on a transfer and on a mint are two separate claims that never collide. Within issuance, however, the namespace is organization-wide: reusing a key for a different issuance operation, even on a different token, returns 409. Issuance keys aren't separated by project either, so never reuse one between your sandbox and production projects.

## This model is open to change

The per-domain differences above reflect the order in which these surfaces shipped, not a finished design. Treat the core contract as stable — one key per logical operation, replay returns the record, payload mismatch returns 409 — and treat the scoping details (per-project vs per-organization namespaces, which endpoints consume the header) as subject to change.

---

### Authentication
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/authentication

> Authenticate API requests with project-scoped API keys, layered with roles, wallet bindings, and network controls.

SDP layers independent controls onto a single API key — role, per-key permissions, wallet bindings, allowed operations, and IP allowlist — so a key grants exactly the access its integration needs, and no more.

Authenticated API requests carry an API key in the `Authorization` header:

```bash title="Terminal"
curl https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```

The `Bearer` prefix is optional — a raw key in the `Authorization` header is also accepted.

## Key scope

Every key is scoped to exactly one **project** and inherits that project's environment: `sk_test_` keys belong to the sandbox project (devnet), `sk_live_` keys to the production project (mainnet-beta). A key can only reach the wallets, tokens, and payments of its own project; there is no cross-project or organization-wide key. Requests for another project's resources return `404`, and `GET /v1/projects` returns only the key's own project. See [Manage API Keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#choose-the-project) for how a key ends up in the sandbox or production project.

## Authorization layers

A request must clear every layer that is configured on its key:

| Layer | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| **Role** | Baseline permission set — see the table below |
| **Per-key permissions** | Optional fine-grained overrides of the role's defaults. A creator can only grant permissions it holds, unless it has `org:admin` (organization admins and `api_admin` keys do) |
| **Wallet bindings** | Restrict which custody wallets the key can operate, each binding with its own permission list |
| **Allowed operations** | Optional allow-list of operation families and types the key may perform on those wallets. Empty means unrestricted |
| **IP allowlist** | Optional IPv4/IPv6/CIDR ranges the key may be used from |

| Role | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `api_admin` | All permissions, including custody administration, token admin operations, and API-key and project management |
| `api_developer` | Read and write access to tokens, payments, counterparties, and wallets, plus read access to compliance. Excludes token admin operations (pause, freeze, seize, force-burn, authority transfer), custody administration, and API-key and project management |
| `api_readonly` | Read-only access to tokens, payments, counterparties, wallets, and compliance. No access to API keys or projects |

Only an `api_admin` key can create or rotate another `api_admin` key.

Allowed operations restrict only requests made with the key; dashboard sessions aren't API keys and aren't restricted by them. A key can only grant operations inside its own list. See [Allowed operations](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#allowed-operations) for the families and how to set them.

## Errors

Authentication and authorization failures are always machine-distinguishable:

| Condition | Status | Code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No API key on a keyed-only request | 401 | `UNAUTHORIZED` |
| Malformed or unknown key | 401 | `INVALID_API_KEY` |
| Key has been revoked | 401 | `REVOKED_API_KEY` |
| Key past its expiry or rotation deadline | 401 | `EXPIRED_API_KEY` |
| Request origin not in the key's IP allowlist | 403 | `FORBIDDEN` |
| Key lacks a required permission | 403 | `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS` |
| Operation not in the key's allowed operations | 403 | `OPERATION_NOT_ALLOWED` |
| Resource belongs to another project | 404 | `NOT_FOUND` |
| Per-key rate limit exceeded | 429 | `RATE_LIMITED` |

Requests are rate limited per key; the standard tier allows 100 requests per minute.

See [Manage API Keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys) for creating, rotating, and revoking keys.

---

### Manage API Keys
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys

> Create, rotate, and revoke API keys with role-based access, wallet bindings, and zero-downtime rotation.

Create, list, rotate, and revoke the API keys that authenticate SDP API requests. Each key belongs to one project, inherits its environment, and carries a role plus optional fine-grained controls — see [Authentication](/docs/developing-with-sdp/authentication) for how those layers are enforced.

The full secret is returned exactly once — at creation and at rotation. SDP stores only a hash and a display prefix; a lost key cannot be recovered, only rotated or replaced. Every key tracks `lastUsedAt` so you can identify stale credentials before revoking them.

## Key format

| Environment | Prefix | Solana network |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sandbox | `sk_test_` | devnet |
| Production | `sk_live_` | mainnet-beta |

## Choose the project

Every organization has a sandbox project and a production project, and a key's environment comes from the project it is created in. No request field sets the environment, and a key can't be moved to another project later.

- **Dashboard:** the key is created in the project selected in the workspace switcher. Switch to the production project before creating a production key.
- **API:** `POST /v1/api-keys` creates the key in the same project as the key that authenticates the request. `POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/api-keys` does the same, and `{projectId}` must be the authenticating key's own project.

An API key can't create keys in the other project, so your first production key has to come from the dashboard. See [Set Up Your Organization & Projects](/docs/guides/setup-organization) for the workspace switcher and production access.

## Roles

| Role | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `api_admin` | All permissions, including custody administration and API-key management |
| `api_developer` | Read and write access to tokens, payments, counterparties, and wallets; no token admin operations, custody administration, or API-key management |
| `api_readonly` | Read-only access to tokens, payments, counterparties, wallets, and compliance |

Managing keys through the API takes the `api-keys:read` and `api-keys:write` permissions. `api_admin` keys have them; `api_developer` and `api_readonly` keys don't. Only an `api_admin` key can create or rotate another `api_admin` key.

A key can also carry explicit `permissions` that override the role's defaults. A creator can only grant permissions it holds, unless it has `org:admin`, as organization admins and `api_admin` keys do.

## Create a key

<Tabs items={["Dashboard", "API"]}>
<Tab value="Dashboard">

Only organization admins can create, rotate, and delete keys in the dashboard; members can view them.

1. In the workspace switcher at the top of the sidebar, select the project the key is for.

2. Navigate to **API keys** in the sidebar. You start with an empty list.

   ![API keys page with no keys yet](/images/getting-started/api-keys-empty.png)

3. Click **Create new API key** (or **New API key** once the project has keys) and work through the four steps:
   - **Details** — a descriptive **Name** (e.g., "CI deploy key") and an optional **Expiration**. The **Environment** is read-only and comes from the selected project.
   - **Permissions** — the role: Admin, Developer, or Read only.
   - **Wallet access** — **All wallets**, or **Selected wallets** with a default signing wallet.
   - **Review** — check the summary and click **Create key**.

4. Click **Copy** on the **API key generated** modal and save the key — it will not be shown again.

   ![API key generated modal showing the full key](/images/getting-started/api-key-generated.png)

5. Dismiss the modal. The key now appears in the table with its prefix, environment, access, and status.

   ![API keys list with one active key](/images/getting-started/api-keys-list.png)

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "CI deploy key",
    "role": "api_developer",
    "walletScope": "all",
    "expiresAt": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="create-api-key.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    name: "CI deploy key",
    role: "api_developer",
    walletScope: "all",
    expiresAt: "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z",
  }),
});
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.apiKey.key — save this, only shown once
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="CreateApiKey.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "name": "CI deploy key",
          "role": "api_developer",
          "walletScope": "all",
          "expiresAt": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z"
        }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The new key belongs to the project of the key that created it and inherits that project's environment — there is no environment field on the request. `POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/api-keys` accepts the same body. The response includes the full `key` value — **save it, it is only returned once**.

`name` and `walletScope` are required; `role` defaults to `api_developer`. Optional fields: `description`, `permissions` (fine-grained overrides), `allowedIps` (IPv4/IPv6/CIDR ranges), `expiresAt`, `signingWalletId` / `signingWalletIds`, `walletBindings` (per-wallet permission lists), `allowedOperations` (see [Allowed operations](#allowed-operations)), and `provisionWallet` with `walletLabel` and `walletPurpose` to create and bind a new custody wallet (requires `custody:admin`). `provisionWallet` names exactly one provider account: `{ "provider": "privy" }` for the project's Managed config for that provider, or `{ "connectionId": "cconn_…" }` for a Custody Connection.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## List keys

`GET /v1/api-keys` lists the keys in the authenticating key's project, newest first; `GET /v1/projects/{projectId}/api-keys` returns the same list for that project. Revoked keys are left out. Each entry carries the `keyPrefix`, `role`, `environment`, `status`, wallet access, `lastUsedAt`, and `expiresAt` — never the secret. `GET /v1/api-keys/{keyId}` returns one key in full, including its `permissions`, `allowedIps`, and rotation details.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="list-api-keys.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys", {
  headers: { "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_..." },
});
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.apiKeys — keys in this project, newest first
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="ListApiKeys.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .GET()
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Allowed operations

A key can carry a list of the operation families and types it may perform on the wallets it can access. The list is an allow-list. An empty or missing list places no restriction. An operation that is not in a non-empty list is refused with `OPERATION_NOT_ALLOWED` before anything executes. Nothing is recorded on refusal, like a missing permission.

| Family | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `payment` | Transfers, transfer batches, and recurring payment creation, updates and collections |
| `ramp` | Ramp quotes |
| `issuance` | Token deploy, mint, burn, seize, force-burn, authority, pause, freeze, metadata and allowlist actions |

The list also accepts the `program` and `privacy` families, which cover operations outside the public API.

Set the list when you create a key, or change it later with `PATCH /v1/api-keys/{keyId}`. A family entry covers every type in it, and a single type can be listed on its own. A key can only grant operations inside its own list.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SDP_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "Payouts worker",
    "walletScope": "selected",
    "signingWalletIds": ["privy_wallet_123"],
    "allowedOperations": ["payment", "ramp_onramp_quote"]
  }'
```

Use `null` or an empty list on update to remove the restriction. Actions that return funds are never restricted by this list.

## Rotate a key

Rotation replaces the secret without an availability gap: the new key is a fresh record that clones the old key's name, role, permissions, IP allowlist, expiry, wallet bindings, and allowed operations, while the old key keeps working until its grace deadline. During the grace period both keys are valid; after it, the old key fails with `EXPIRED_API_KEY`. A key can be rotated once: rotating it again while its replacement is active returns `409 CONFLICT` naming the replacement.

<Tabs items={["Dashboard", "API"]}>
<Tab value="Dashboard">

1. In the API keys table, open the **Actions** dropdown next to the key and click **Rotate key (24h grace)**. The dashboard always uses a 24-hour grace period — use the API for a custom value (0–168h).

   ![Actions dropdown showing Rotate key and Delete key options](/images/getting-started/api-key-rotate.png)

2. Copy the new key value from the generated key modal — it is shown once.

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys/key_abc123/rotate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "gracePeriodHours": 24 }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="rotate-api-key.ts"
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys/key_abc123/rotate",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ gracePeriodHours: 24 }),
  }
);
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.apiKey — the new key, only shown once
// data.previousKey.rotationDeadline — when the old key stops working
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="RotateApiKey.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys/key_abc123/rotate"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        { "gracePeriodHours": 24 }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

`gracePeriodHours` accepts 0–168 (default 24). A key cannot rotate itself — authenticate the rotation with a different key in the same project, or rotate from the dashboard.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Revoke a key

<Tabs items={["Dashboard", "API"]}>
<Tab value="Dashboard">

Open the **Actions** dropdown next to the key and click **Delete key**, then type the key's name to confirm. The key stops working immediately and cannot be restored.

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X DELETE https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys/key_abc123 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "confirmation": "CI deploy key" }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="revoke-api-key.ts"
await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys/key_abc123", {
  method: "DELETE",
  headers: {
    "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ confirmation: "CI deploy key" }),
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="RevokeApiKey.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/api-keys/key_abc123"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .method("DELETE", HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        { "confirmation": "CI deploy key" }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The `confirmation` field must match the key's **name**. Revocation takes effect immediately, is idempotent (revoking an already-revoked key succeeds), and cannot be undone. As with rotation, a key cannot revoke itself.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

---

### Signing modes
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/signing-modes

> When SDP signs and submits a transaction for you, and when it returns an unsigned transaction for you to sign and submit.

Every SDP operation that changes on-chain state ends in a Solana transaction that someone has to sign. SDP offers two ways to get there:

- **Execute:** SDP builds the transaction, signs it with a custody wallet in your project, submits it, and records the result. Most routes work this way.
- **Prepare:** SDP builds the transaction and returns it unsigned. You sign it, submit it to Solana yourself, and track the result. Prepare routes have `prepare` in their path.

## Which operations support which mode

| Operation | Execute | Prepare |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Token deploy | `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/deploy` | — |
| Mint, burn | `POST .../mint`, `POST .../burn` | `POST .../mint/prepare`, `POST .../burn/prepare` |
| Seize, force burn | `POST .../seize`, `POST .../force-burn` | `POST .../seize/prepare`, `POST .../force-burn/prepare` |
| Authority transfer | `POST .../authority` | `POST .../authority/prepare` |
| Pause, unpause, freeze, unfreeze, allowlist changes | Yes | No |
| Transfers and transfer batches | `POST /v1/payments/transfers`, `POST /v1/payments/transfer-batches` | No |
| Recurring payments | `/v1/payments/recurring-payments` routes | No |

For mint, burn, seize, force burn, and authority transfer, the prepare route takes the same request body as the execute route.

## Execute

On an execute route, SDP runs the whole transaction itself:

1. It checks the API key's permissions and its access to the custody wallet that will sign.
2. Issuance execute routes, transfers, transfer batches, and the recurring payment create, update, and collect routes also check the key's [allowed operations](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys#allowed-operations). An operation outside a non-empty list is refused with `403 OPERATION_NOT_ALLOWED`, and nothing is signed.
3. SDP signs with the custody wallet and submits the transaction.
4. The response carries the operation record with its on-chain `signature` and `status`. A transfer can come back `processing` while SDP is still confirming it; don't create a replacement transfer for it.

Transfers, transfer batches, and most issuance execute routes accept an `Idempotency-Key` header, so a retried request returns the original record instead of signing again. See [Idempotency](/docs/developing-with-sdp/idempotency) for the list.

## Prepare

Every prepare response carries the unsigned transaction in the same shape:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `serialized` | Base64-encoded wire-format transaction with empty signature slots |
| `blockhash` | Recent blockhash the transaction was built with |
| `lastValidBlockHeight` | Last block height at which the transaction can land, as a decimal string |

Submit the signed transaction before the cluster passes `lastValidBlockHeight`. After that it can't land, and you need to prepare a new one.

Prepare routes differ from execute routes in three ways:

- **No allowed-operations check.** Allowed operations restrict execute routes only, so a key whose list leaves out mint can still call `mint/prepare`. Permission checks, wallet access checks, and issuance token rules such as control lists and maximum supply still run.
- **No idempotent replay.** Prepare routes don't use `Idempotency-Key`. Every call builds a new transaction and creates a new operation record.
- **SDP doesn't submit.** You submit the signed transaction to Solana and check the outcome on-chain; SDP isn't told whether it landed.

### Issuance: mint, burn, seize, force burn, authority

The response contains:

- `transaction`: the SDP operation record for this operation, created with status `pending`
- `preparedTransaction`: the unsigned transaction
- `simulation`: present when you set `options.simulate` to `true`
- `tokenAccount` (mint only): the destination's token account

**Who signs.** The custody wallet in your project that holds the authority for the operation: the mint authority for mint, the permanent delegate for seize and force burn, the authority being changed for an authority transfer, and the wallet that owns the tokens for burn. To choose it, pass the SDP Wallet `id` (`cwlt_…` from `GET /v1/wallets`) as `signingCustodyWalletId`. It's required for burn and optional for the others. The same wallet is the fee payer: it pays the network fee, and for mint the rent for a new destination token account. SDP doesn't sponsor fees on prepared issuance transactions. The key for this wallet lives with your custody provider, so the signing step happens outside SDP.

**Who submits.** You do. No route reports the result back to SDP, so the operation record stays `pending`. Use the signature returned when you submit to check the outcome on-chain. After a mint or burn lands, `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/supply/refresh` re-reads the token's supply from the chain.

**Maximum supply.** A prepared mint counts against the token's maximum supply as soon as SDP returns it, because it can still land until its blockhash expires. If the amount would exceed the cap, the request fails with `MAX_SUPPLY_EXCEEDED`.

**Permissions.** Mint and burn need `tokens:write`. Seize, force burn, and authority transfer need `tokens:admin`. The API key must also have access to the signing wallet with that permission.

**Rate limit.** Issuance prepare routes share a separate quota of 30 requests per minute per API key and 120 per organization. Requests over the quota return `429 RATE_LIMITED`.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_123/mint/prepare \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "mint": {
      "destination": "7xKXtg2CW87d97TXJSDpbD5jBkheTqA83TZRuJosgAsU",
      "amount": "100"
    },
    "options": { "simulate": true }
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="prepare-mint.ts"
  createSolanaRpc,
  getBase64EncodedWireTransaction,
  getBase64Encoder,
  getTransactionDecoder,
} from "@solana/kit";

const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/issuance/tokens/tok_123/mint/prepare",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      mint: {
        destination: "7xKXtg2CW87d97TXJSDpbD5jBkheTqA83TZRuJosgAsU",
        amount: "100",
      },
      options: { simulate: true },
    }),
  }
);
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.transaction: the SDP operation record (status "pending")
// data.preparedTransaction: { serialized, blockhash, lastValidBlockHeight }

const unsigned = getTransactionDecoder().decode(
  getBase64Encoder().encode(data.preparedTransaction.serialized)
);

// Placeholder: sign with the custody wallet that holds the mint authority,
// through your custody provider's own signing API.
const signed = await signWithCustodyWallet(unsigned);

const rpc = createSolanaRpc("https://api.devnet.solana.com");
const signature = await rpc
  .sendTransaction(getBase64EncodedWireTransaction(signed), { encoding: "base64" })
  .send();
// Check the outcome on-chain with this signature; SDP isn't told about it.
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Choosing a mode

| If you need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| SDP to sign with a custody wallet, submit, and return the recorded result | Execute |
| The key's allowed operations to apply | Execute. Prepare routes don't check allowed operations. |
| Safe retries after timeouts | Execute with an `Idempotency-Key` |
| SDP to keep the operation record up to date | Execute. Prepared issuance records stay `pending`. |
| Fee sponsorship | Execute. SDP doesn't sponsor prepared issuance transactions. |
| The unsigned transaction, to inspect or simulate before you sign it with the custody wallet's key outside SDP | Prepare |
| Pause, freeze, allowlist changes, transfers, transfer batches, or recurring payments | Execute. These operations have no prepare route. |

---

### API playground
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/developing-with-sdp/api-playground

> Send live API requests from the dashboard with one of your project's API keys.

The dashboard has an API playground on several module pages. You pick an endpoint, fill in its parameters and request body, and run it against the SDP API with one of your project's API keys. The playground doesn't simulate anything: every request it sends is a real API call.

## Where to find it

Open one of the pages below and select the **API Playground** tab next to **Overview**. A page appears only when its module is enabled for your organization. The tab is hidden on screens narrower than 768 pixels.

| Dashboard page | Endpoints in the playground |
| --- | --- |
| **Wallets** | Wallet endpoints under `/v1/wallets` |
| **Issuance** | Issuance endpoints under `/v1/issuance`, including the prepare routes next to their execute routes |
| **Payments** | Payments endpoints under `/v1/payments`, such as transfers, transfer batches, and recurring payments |
| **Counterparty** (in Payments) | Counterparty endpoints under `/v1/counterparties` |

Choose an endpoint from the list, edit the path parameters and the JSON body, and click **Run request**. The playground shows the HTTP status and the response body. The selected endpoint is kept in the page URL, so you can share a link to it.

On **Issuance** and **Payments**, the endpoint selected when you open the tab is a write endpoint: `POST /v1/issuance/tokens/{tokenId}/mint` and `POST /v1/payments/transfers`. Nothing is sent until you click **Run request**.

## What a request runs as

**Your API key, not your dashboard sign-in.** Paste the full secret of an API key (`sk_test_…` or `sk_live_…`) into the key field. When you leave the field, the dashboard checks that the key belongs to the project you have selected and is active and unexpired, then shows which key it is. A key from another project is rejected. Each request then runs with that key's role, permissions, and wallet access, as if your own code had sent it.

If the project has no API keys, the field is replaced by a **Create API key** link for users who can manage keys. When you create a key in the dashboard, the playground picks it up without pasting, under the same clearing rules as a pasted key.

**The key's environment.** The key decides where a request runs: an `sk_test_` key belongs to a sandbox project on devnet, and an `sk_live_` key to a production project on mainnet-beta. The playground doesn't show the environment separately, so check the key prefix before you run a write request.

**Real execution.** Requests go from the dashboard's server to the SDP API. Only `/v1/` paths are allowed. Write requests change your data, and execute endpoints sign and submit transactions with your custody wallets. The playground has no confirmation step before a write request and doesn't send an `Idempotency-Key` header. Prepare endpoints return an unsigned transaction, which the playground doesn't sign or submit. They still have the side effects described in [Signing modes](/docs/developing-with-sdp/signing-modes).

**Where the key is kept.** The pasted key stays in your browser tab's memory and isn't written to browser storage. It's cleared after 15 minutes of inactivity, when you switch organization or project, and when you sign out.

## Copying a request

- **Copy Code** copies the current request as a JavaScript `fetch` snippet, with a placeholder where your API key goes.
- **AI instructions** copies a prompt that describes the endpoint, its parameters, and the request body.

## Playground, API reference, and Postman collection

The playground's endpoint lists are generated from the same public OpenAPI document as the [API reference](/docs/reference/api) and the [Postman collection](/docs/reference/postman-collection), and some dashboard pages add hand-written entries on top. Each tool suits a different job:

| Tool | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| API playground | Try an endpoint in the dashboard against the project you have selected, with one of its keys |
| API reference | Browse every public endpoint by family, with the full schemas in the [OpenAPI document](https://api.solana.com/openapi.json) |
| Postman collection | Run and save requests outside the dashboard, against any environment you set in `baseUrl` with the key you set in `sdpApiKey` |

The playground covers fewer endpoint groups than the API reference: it has no tab for health, API keys, projects, compliance, or asset profiles, and it lists only endpoints that accept API key authentication.

---

## Getting Started

### Set Up Your Organization & Projects
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/guides/setup-organization

> Create your SDP organization, work in its sandbox and production projects, and invite your team.

Every SDP user works through an **organization**, your team's shared account. Each organization has exactly two **projects**: a sandbox project and a production project. A project has its own API keys, wallets, tokens, and payments, so testing in sandbox never touches production. This guide creates your organization, explains the two projects, and shows how to bring in your team.

## Create your organization

### 1. Sign up

Go to [platform.solana.com](https://platform.solana.com) and click **Dashboard**. On the sign-in screen, click **Sign up** to create a new account.

![SDP sign-in screen with Sign up link](/images/getting-started/sign-in.png)

Enter your email address and a password to create your account.

![Create your account screen](/images/getting-started/create-account.png)

### 2. Create the organization

After signing in you'll be prompted to set up your organization. Upload a logo and enter your organization name, then click **Continue**.

![Setup your organization screen](/images/getting-started/setup-organization.png)

If a teammate has already invited you, accept their invitation to join their organization instead of creating a new one.

SDP creates the organization's sandbox and production projects the first time you open the dashboard. Every member of the organization has access to both.

## Sandbox and production projects

| Project | `environment` | Solana network | API key prefix | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sandbox | `sandbox` | devnet | `sk_test_` | Building and testing your integration |
| Production | `production` | mainnet-beta | `sk_live_` | Live operations on mainnet |

You can't create, delete, or archive projects; every organization has exactly these two. You can rename a project or change its description.

Each project sets up its own custody providers. The production project can only create wallets in custody connections that use your own provider credentials; see [Set Up Wallets](/docs/guides/setup-wallets#custody-modes).

The production project is available once production access is enabled for your organization. Until then, the dashboard lists only the sandbox project and `GET /v1/projects` leaves production out. Contact the SDP team to enable production.

## Switch between projects

The workspace switcher at the top of the dashboard sidebar shows your organization's name above the active project's name. Open it to:

- switch to another organization you belong to
- select the project to work in, listed under **Projects**
- copy your organization ID

Wallets, tokens, payments, and API keys in the dashboard always belong to the selected project. The project is part of the page URL, so each browser tab stays in its own project and a shared link opens the same project for anyone who can access it. Opening the dashboard without a project takes you to the project you last used, or to sandbox.

## Invite your team

Organization admins manage members on the **Settings** page, which opens from the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar.

1. Click your name at the bottom of the sidebar and choose **Settings**.
2. Under **Members**, enter your teammate's email address, choose a role, and click **Send invite**.
3. The invitation is listed as **Pending** until it's accepted. Its actions menu lets you **Copy invite link** or **Revoke invite**.

| Role | Access |
| --- | --- |
| **Admin** | Full organization control: create, rotate, and delete API keys, invite and remove members, and manage custody, including creating wallets and custody connections |
| **Member** | Works with tokens, payments, counterparties, and existing wallets, and can view API keys, but can't create or change keys, create wallets, manage custody, or invite members |

Members you invite get access to both projects. To remove someone, open the actions menu on their row and click **Remove member**; they lose access to the organization immediately. You can't remove yourself or the organization's last admin.

## API keys belong to one project

Every API key belongs to exactly one project and inherits its environment. There is no organization-wide key.

- **In the dashboard**, a new key is created in the project selected in the workspace switcher. Switch to the production project before creating a production key.
- **Through the API**, a new key lands in the same project as the key that creates it. A key can't create keys in, or read data from, the other project.

That means your first production key comes from the dashboard. See [Manage API Keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys) for the full flow.

## Projects API

Use the Projects endpoints to read project details and manage the keys in a project:

| Endpoint | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/projects` | Lists the organization's projects. With an API key, it returns only that key's project |
| `GET /v1/projects/{projectId}` | Returns one project |
| `PATCH /v1/projects/{projectId}` | Updates the project's name, description, or settings |
| `GET /v1/projects/{projectId}/provider-availability` | Lists the custody, compliance, and ramp providers the deployment knows, with whether the project can use each one |
| `GET /v1/projects/{projectId}/members` | Lists the project's members |
| `GET /v1/projects/{projectId}/api-keys` | Lists the project's API keys, excluding revoked ones |
| `POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/api-keys` | Creates an API key in the project |

With an API key, `{projectId}` must be the key's own project; any other ID returns 404. Any key of the project can read provider availability. The other endpoints need project and API-key permissions that `api_admin` keys have and `api_developer` and `api_readonly` keys don't.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl https://api.solana.com/v1/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="list-projects.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/projects", {
  headers: { "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_..." },
});
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.projects — with an API key, only the key's own project
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="ListProjects.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/projects"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .GET()
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "projects": [
      {
        "id": "prj_3bc13bcb-...",
        "name": "Default Sandbox Project",
        "slug": "default-sandbox",
        "environment": "sandbox",
        "status": "active"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

See the [Projects API reference](/docs/reference/api/projects) for every field and endpoint.

## Next steps

- [Set up wallets](/docs/guides/setup-wallets) for signing transactions
- [Create API keys](/docs/developing-with-sdp/manage-api-keys) for programmatic access
- [Create your first token](/docs/tokens/create-a-token)

### Set Up Wallets
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/guides/setup-wallets

> Set up a custody provider in your project and create wallets for signing transactions.

A **custody wallet** is a Solana keypair whose key is held and signed for by a custody provider — SDP routes signing requests to whichever provider holds the wallet's key. Set up a provider in your project, then create wallets for token deployment, minting, transfers, and other onchain operations.

Custody belongs to a project. The sandbox and production projects each set up their own providers and hold their own wallets. There is no default provider and no default wallet: every wallet names the provider account it lives in, and every operation that signs names its wallet.

## Custody modes

A wallet lives in one of two kinds of provider account, fixed when it is created:

| Mode | Where the wallet lives | Projects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Managed** | The provider account the SDP deployment holds. You set it up from the dashboard or with `POST /v1/wallets/initialize`, and create wallets in it with `provider`. | Sandbox only |
| **Bring your own credentials** | A **custody connection**: a provider account your team owns, connected with credentials you store in SDP. You add it from the dashboard and create wallets in it with `connectionId`. Privy is the only provider that supports connections today. | Sandbox and production |

A production project uses custody connections only. To add one, see [Custody connections](/docs/guides/integrations#custody-connections).

## Supported providers

Use the `provider` value when you set up Managed custody or create a Managed wallet through the API.

| Provider | `provider` value | Signs transactions | Modes | Access |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Privy** | `privy` | Yes | Managed, bring your own credentials | Every organization |
| **Coinbase CDP** | `coinbase_cdp` | Yes | Managed | Every organization |
| **Para** | `para` | Yes | Managed | Every organization |
| **Turnkey** | `turnkey` | Yes | Managed | Every organization |
| **Fireblocks** | `fireblocks` | Yes | Managed | By arrangement |
| **DFNS** | `dfns` | Yes | Managed | By arrangement |
| **IBM Digital Asset Haven** | `ibm_haven` | Yes | Managed | By arrangement |
| **Utila** | `utila` | Yes | Managed | By arrangement |
| **Anchorage** | `anchorage` | No | Managed | By arrangement |
| **Local Signer** | `local` | Yes | Managed | Self-hosted deployments only |

- **Every organization**: your organization has access without asking for it.
- **By arrangement**: the SDP team has to grant your organization access first.
- **Anchorage**: SDP can create and delete Anchorage wallets, but it does not sign transactions with them.
- **Local Signer**: SDP generates the wallet's key and stores it encrypted in the deployment's database. It holds one wallet per project and can't create more. Only a [self-hosted](/docs/self-hosting) deployment with `CUSTODY_PRIVATE_KEY` set offers it, and the operator enables it per organization.

### Which providers a project can use

A project can use a provider in a mode when all of these checks pass, in this order. The first check that fails is the reason SDP reports:

| Check | Reason when it fails |
| --- | --- |
| The deployment's release channel offers the provider in that mode. | `custody_provider_not_in_release_channel` |
| The project's environment allows the mode: Managed in sandbox only, bring your own credentials in both. | `custody_mode_not_allowed` |
| Your organization has access to the provider. | `provider_not_entitled` |
| Managed only: the deployment holds the provider's credentials. | `provider_not_configured` |

In a production project, that leaves custody connections, so Privy is the only provider a production project can use.

The dashboard lists only the providers the project can use in at least one mode; a provider the project can't use isn't shown. A request that sets up or uses an unavailable provider is refused with `403` and `details.reason` set to the failed check, or with `503` when the deployment doesn't hold the provider's credentials.

To check through the API, read the project's provider availability. Any API key of the project can read it, and `{projectId}` must be the key's own project; any other ID returns `404`.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl https://api.solana.com/v1/projects/prj_123/provider-availability \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_..."
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="provider-availability.ts"
const response = await fetch(
  "https://api.solana.com/v1/projects/prj_123/provider-availability",
  { headers: { "Authorization": "Bearer sk_live_..." } },
);
const { data } = await response.json();
// data: { projectId, environment, providers }
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="ProviderAvailability.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/projects/prj_123/provider-availability"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_live_...")
    .GET()
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The response lists every custody, compliance, and ramp provider the deployment knows. A custody entry lists the modes the project can use in `modes`, which is empty when there are none, and the first failed check for each other mode in `unavailableModes`:

```json title="response.json"
{
  "data": {
    "projectId": "prj_123",
    "environment": "production",
    "providers": [
      {
        "family": "custody",
        "provider": "privy",
        "modes": ["byok"],
        "unavailableModes": [{ "mode": "managed", "reason": "custody_mode_not_allowed" }]
      },
      {
        "family": "custody",
        "provider": "fireblocks",
        "modes": [],
        "unavailableModes": [
          { "mode": "managed", "reason": "custody_mode_not_allowed" },
          { "mode": "byok", "reason": "custody_provider_not_in_release_channel" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

`byok` is the API's name for bring your own credentials. Compliance and ramp entries carry `available` instead, plus a `reason` when it is `false`.

## Create wallets

<Tabs items={["Dashboard", "API"]}>
<Tab value="Dashboard">

### 1. Open Wallets

Open the sidebar and click **Wallets**. The page shows the wallets of the project selected in the workspace switcher; see [Set Up Your Organization & Projects](/docs/guides/setup-organization#switch-between-projects). Only organization admins can create wallets. Members see the project's wallets but can't create new ones.

### 2. Choose a custody provider

If the project has no wallets yet, the page shows **Create your first wallet** with a card for each provider the project can use. Click the provider's card.

If the project already has wallets, click **Create wallet**, pick a provider under **Choose provider**, and click **Next**.

A provider the project already uses for Managed custody is marked **Active**. If no provider is available to the project, the page says so instead of listing providers.

### 3. Create the wallet

Under **Wallet details**, enter a **Wallet label** and click **Create wallet**. Depending on the provider and the project, this step also asks:

- **Custody mode**: shown when the provider isn't set up in the project yet and can run either way, such as Privy in a sandbox project. Choose **Managed** or **Bring your own credentials**.
- **Provider details**: bring your own credentials replaces the wallet form with a form for your own Privy app. In a production project with no Privy connection yet, Privy goes straight to this form. See [Custody connections](/docs/guides/integrations#custody-connections).
- **Account**: shown when the provider has an active custody connection. Choose the account the wallet is created in: **Managed by SDP**, when the project uses that provider for Managed custody, or one of the connections. Nothing is preselected, because every wallet names where it lives. Connections that aren't ready yet are listed but can't be chosen.

### 4. View your wallet

After provisioning, the wallet's card appears on the Wallets page with its provider, label, balance, address, and wallet ID. Click the card to open the wallet's page.

To create more wallets, click **Create wallet** and repeat the process.

### 5. Provider capabilities

A provider's page under **Integrations** → **Custody** lists its capabilities. **Issuance**, **Transfers**, and **Compliance** name the SDP features its wallets are meant for. **Transaction signing** and **Additional wallets** appear when the provider signs transactions and can create more than one wallet.

</Tab>
<Tab value="API">

#### 1. Set up Managed custody

In a sandbox project, set up Managed custody with a provider. SDP creates the project's signing configuration for that provider and its first wallet.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets/initialize \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "provider": "privy",
    "walletLabel": "Master wallet"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="initialize-wallet-provider.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets/initialize", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    provider: "privy",
    walletLabel: "Master wallet",
  }),
});
const { data } = await response.json();
// data: { configId, publicKey, walletId }
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="InitializeWalletProvider.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets/initialize"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "provider": "privy",
          "walletLabel": "Master wallet"
        }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

- The API key needs the `custody:admin` permission, which `api_admin` keys have. Keys scoped to selected wallets (`"walletScope": "selected"`) are refused.
- Production projects use bring your own credentials only, so in a production project this returns `403` with `details.reason` set to `custody_mode_not_allowed`. Create wallets in a custody connection instead; see [Create a wallet on a custody connection](#create-a-wallet-on-a-custody-connection).
- If the project already has Managed custody with that provider, the request returns `409`. Create more wallets with `POST /v1/wallets`.

#### 2. Create additional wallets

Every wallet names the provider account it lives under: `provider` for the project's Managed custody with that provider, or `connectionId` for a custody connection. Send exactly one of them; a body with both or neither returns `400`. This example creates a Managed wallet:

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "provider": "privy",
    "label": "Mint authority wallet",
    "purpose": "mint_authority"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="create-wallet.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    provider: "privy",
    label: "Mint authority wallet",
    purpose: "mint_authority",
  }),
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="CreateWallet.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "provider": "privy",
          "label": "Mint authority wallet",
          "purpose": "mint_authority"
        }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

`provider` needs Managed custody with that provider in the project; without it, the request returns `404`. The API key needs the same permission as step 1. The `purpose` field is optional metadata in the API. The current dashboard create-wallet flow does not expose wallet-purpose selection.

#### 3. List wallets

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl "https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets?view=summary" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..."
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="list-wallets.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets?view=summary", {
  headers: { "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_..." },
});
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.wallets includes id, walletId, publicKey, provider, label, purpose, and status
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="ListWallets.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets?view=summary"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .GET()
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Each wallet carries `custodyConfigId` when it is Managed, or `custodyConnectionId` when it lives in a custody connection.

Every operation that signs names its wallet; there is no default wallet. Transfers take the wallet's `id` (`cwlt_…`) as `sourceCustodyWalletId`, and issuance takes it as `signingCustodyWalletId`. Wallet-scoped API keys bind the wallet's `walletId` in `signingWalletIds`.

```typescript title="transfer-request.ts"
const body = {
  sourceCustodyWalletId: "cwlt_123", // `id` from GET /v1/wallets
  destination: "7xKXz...9fGh",
  token: "9aBCd...4eEf",
  amount: "100.00",
};
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Create a wallet on a custody connection

A custody connection is added in the dashboard; see [Custody connections](/docs/guides/integrations#custody-connections). Once it is active, create wallets in it by passing its `connectionId` instead of `provider`. This works in sandbox and production projects.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "connectionId": "cconn_123",
    "label": "Treasury wallet"
  }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="create-connection-wallet.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Authorization": "Bearer sk_live_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    connectionId: "cconn_123",
    label: "Treasury wallet",
  }),
});
const { data } = await response.json();
// data.wallet.custodyConnectionId === "cconn_123"
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="CreateConnectionWallet.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_live_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        {
          "connectionId": "cconn_123",
          "label": "Treasury wallet"
        }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The created wallet carries `custodyConnectionId` instead of `custodyConfigId`, and signs with the connection's credentials. To find a connection's ID, open **Integrations** → **Custody** → **Privy** in the dashboard, open the connection, and copy its **Connection ID**.

The request fails when:

| Status | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | The body names both `connectionId` and `provider`, or neither. |
| `403` | The API key lacks `custody:admin` or is scoped to selected wallets. Also returned with `details.reason` `custody_provider_not_in_release_channel` when the deployment's release channel doesn't offer the provider for connections, or `provider_not_entitled` when your organization no longer has access to it. |
| `404` | No connection with that ID exists in the API key's project. |
| `409` | The connection isn't active: its verification is unfinished or failed, or it or its credentials were deactivated. |
| `503` | The provider or the stored credentials couldn't be reached. |

To give a new API key its own wallet in a connection, pass `"provisionWallet": { "connectionId": "..." }` on `POST /v1/api-keys`, or `{ "provider": "..." }` for a Managed wallet. See the [API keys reference](/docs/reference/api/api-keys).

## Check signer readiness

`POST /v1/wallets/signer-check` confirms that SDP can sign with a wallet before you rely on it. SDP builds a memo transaction with server-generated text, asks the custody provider to sign it with the wallet, verifies the signature, and simulates the transaction. Nothing is broadcast and no fees are spent.

Pass the provider wallet ID, which is the `walletId` field from `GET /v1/wallets` (for example `privy_wallet_123`), not the record `id` (`cwlt_…`). You can leave `walletId` out when the API key has a signing wallet (`signingWalletId`) or is bound to exactly one wallet; SDP then checks that wallet.

<Tabs items={["curl", "TypeScript", "Java"]}>
<Tab value="curl">
```bash title="Terminal"
curl -X POST https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets/signer-check \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_test_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "walletId": "privy_wallet_123" }'
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="TypeScript">
```typescript title="signer-check.ts"
const response = await fetch("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets/signer-check", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Authorization": "Bearer sk_test_...",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ walletId: "privy_wallet_123" }),
});
const { data } = await response.json();
// data: { walletId, walletAddress, feePayer, memo, signature, simulated, checkedAt }
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Java">
```java title="SignerCheck.java"
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
    .uri(URI.create("https://api.solana.com/v1/wallets/signer-check"))
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_test_...")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("""
        { "walletId": "privy_wallet_123" }"""))
    .build();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

A `200` response means the provider returned a valid signature and the transaction passed simulation. `simulated` is always `true`, and the returned `signature` never appears on chain. If the provider can't sign, returns an invalid signature, or simulation fails, the request returns an error instead.

- The API key needs the `wallets:write` permission.
- Signer checks have a small quota: 2 per minute per API key or user, and 10 per minute per organization. Requests over the quota return `429`.

See the [Wallets API reference](/docs/reference/api/wallets) for every wallet endpoint.

---

### Integrations
Source: https://platform.solana.com/docs/guides/integrations

> Connect your own custody provider account and see the custody, compliance, and ramp providers your project can use.

SDP works with outside providers for custody, compliance screening, and fiat ramps. This guide covers what the dashboard's **Integrations** page shows, how to connect your own custody provider account, and which parts you can also use through the API.

## Where integrations live

In the dashboard sidebar, open **Integrations**. The page, and the sidebar entry's submenu, list one family each: **Custody**, **Ramps**, and **Compliance**. A family appears when its module is turned on for your deployment. Choose a family to see its providers as cards.

The page shows the project selected in the workspace switcher, and lists only the providers that project can use. A provider the project can't use is hidden rather than shown as unavailable. Each card shows a status:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Connected** | The project uses this custody provider for Managed custody. |
| **Ready to connect** | The project can set this custody provider up now. |
| **Enabled** | A ramp or compliance provider the project can use. The deployment provides it, so there is nothing to connect. |

Click a card to open the provider's page. It describes the provider and has a **How it connects** section. A custody provider's page also lists its capabilities, and its header offers the next step: **Configure** opens wallet setup with the provider selected, and **Manage**, shown once the provider is Connected, opens **Wallets**.

The same availability is in the API: `GET /v1/projects/{projectId}/provider-availability` lists every custody, compliance, and ramp provider the deployment knows, with whether the project can use it. See [Which providers a project can use](/docs/guides/setup-wallets#which-providers-a-project-can-use).

## Custody

Custody providers hold your wallets' keys and sign for them. You set them up from **Wallets**, and the **Custody** family lists the same providers. For the provider list, which providers sign transactions, and what decides whether a project can use each one, see [Set Up Wallets](/docs/guides/setup-wallets#supported-providers).

A custody provider's **How it connects** section says how it is set up:

- **Self-serve**: you connect it with credentials from your own provider account. Today this applies to Privy.
- **By arrangement**: the SDP team grants your organization access and sets up the connection. This applies to Fireblocks, DFNS, IBM Digital Asset Haven, Anchorage, and Utila.
- **Provisioned per deployment**: the deployment's operator configures the provider. This applies to Coinbase CDP, Para, Turnkey, and Local Signer.

### Custody connections

A **custody connection** links the project to a provider account your team owns, using credentials you store in SDP. Wallets created in a connection sign with its credentials. Privy is the only provider that supports connections today. A connection belongs to one project, and a project can have several.

Connections are the only custody a production project can use: Managed custody, which runs on the deployment's own provider accounts, is available in sandbox projects only. A sandbox project can use both.

You manage connections in the dashboard, signed in as a user with custody admin access, which organization admins have. API keys can't add or change connections. Other members see a note that managing connections needs the custody admin role.

To connect a Privy app:

1. Open **Integrations** → **Custody** → **Privy**. In the **Connections** section, click **Add connection**.

   The first time you set Privy up in a project, you can also start from **Wallets** by choosing Privy when you create a wallet. If the project can use Privy either way, choose **Bring your own credentials** under **Custody mode**; otherwise the wizard goes straight to the credential form.
2. Enter:
   - **Credential label**: a name for this credential.
   - **Privy app ID**: from your Privy dashboard. After you save, SDP shows only redacted details.
   - **Privy app secret**: from your Privy dashboard. You can't view it again after saving.
   - **Initial wallet label** (optional): a name for the wallet SDP creates when the check succeeds.
3. Click **Connect and verify**. SDP stores the credential, checks it with Privy, and creates the connection's first wallet once the check succeeds.

If the check doesn't succeed, the dashboard says why:

- Privy rejected the credentials: correct the app ID and secret, then connect again.
- The Privy app is already connected to a custody setup: use a different Privy app.
- SDP couldn't confirm whether verification finished: click **Check again**. Your credentials are stored, and checking again never creates a duplicate connection.

Open a connection from the **Connections** list to manage it:

- **Connection ID**: copy it to [create wallets in this connection](/docs/guides/setup-wallets#create-a-wallet-on-a-custody-connection) through the API.
- **Add wallet**: creates a wallet in this connection's Privy account. Available while the connection is active.
- **Rotate credentials**: replaces the stored Privy credentials. Enter the app ID and the new app secret. If Privy rejects them, the current credentials stay in use. Rotation applies to every connection that uses the same credentials, and you can **Roll back** to the previous secret until the rollback window shown on the page ends.
- **Check again** and **Cancel setup**: for a connection whose verification didn't finish. Checking again continues the same setup. Cancelling deactivates the connection, which stays listed as **Deactivated**; to try again, add a new connection.
- **Deactivate connection**: stops the connection permanently and keeps its history. It doesn't revoke the app secret at Privy, and it isn't available while the connection has active wallets.

## Compliance screening

SDP screens addresses through these providers:

| Provider | `provider` value in results |
| --- | --- |
| **Range** | `range` |
| **Elliptic** | `elliptic` |
| **TRM Labs** | `trm` |
| **Chainalysis** | `chainalysis` |

The SDP team activates compliance providers per organization. The **Compliance** family lists each provider your project can use as **Enabled**; a provider that isn't activated for your organization isn't listed.
